segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Garret Marsh put his horse across the tail of the cart before the buyer in the grey coat could lay the next two bundles in the crate.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Stop your counting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The driver came round the wheel with the tally board still in his hand and told him the crate was paid for at the loading. Garret did not look at him.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Pay for it after. Hear the girl, and then count.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Elin Hargrove got down and came to the crate with a leaf in each hand. Carters and a bridge warden drifted over from the ford to watch, the way men do when somebody stops a cart.

segments.speaker: Elin Hargrove
segments.text: This one is off my master's own cord, cut this autumn. Watch the glass, not me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She breathed on it. The mist came up grey across the vein and thinned away again while she held it out at arm's length. Then she took the leaf from Jasper Lund's rack between two fingers and breathed on that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fog sat on it like breath on a window latch. She counted aloud to ten. It was still sitting there at ten, and the vein underneath it shone as bright as a new coin.

segments.speaker: Elin Hargrove
segments.text: Now rub it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The buyer rubbed it. He looked at the silver on his thumb for a long moment, then wiped his hand down his coat.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Whortle-berry and ash water. Forty cords of it, and a trader three days back who very nearly didn't come out of a hollow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The buyer stepped back from the crate and told the driver to load it all again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The driver swore at the horses instead of the men, which was the nearest thing to restraint anyone saw that afternoon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Dessa Fenwick spoke up from her saddle.

segments.speaker: Dessa Fenwick
segments.text: Whose mark is burned on every tag in that crate?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The driver did not need to read it. Mabel Odell's mark went back up the hill unsold, and the loss came off her credit in Tollgate, where she had spent eleven years building it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Earlmere, four days later, half the street stood at Mabel's counter wanting Jasper Lund's grove sold to cover what the town had lost. Mabel let them talk themselves hoarse. Garret waited by the fire until they had finished.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Sell the grove and you've a man with nothing, and nothing is what makes a painted leaf. He cuts under me. Every bundle he brings, he brings to my shed, and I weigh it and I pass it. Three seasons, and the debt comes off in leaf.

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: And the draught from Tollgate? It comes every ten days.

segments.speaker: Mabel Odell
segments.text: Advanced against your cut, and written in my book where anybody may read it. Your wage will be poor and your mother will have her medicine.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jasper looked at the floorboards and said that he would take it. Nobody shook his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Glasswood Society met at the end of the month in the old sawmill office at Earlmere, six of them round a table, with Garret standing because he had never once sat down in that room. He put the two leaves on the table, the warm one and the cold one.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Write it as the breath test. A ripe leaf takes the mist off itself in a count of three. A green one holds it, dye or no dye. We've run it forty times now and it has not missed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The clerk asked whose finding it was, pen already down on the page.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Elin Hargrove's. Nineteen years old, miller's daughter, and my apprentice as of this morning if she'll have the work.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Elin opened her mouth and, for once in her life, shut it again.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Twenty-two years I cut in that wood and I never thought to breathe on one. Go on. You write it down. It's your hand it belongs in.
